title: Cavity collapse and kinetic energy concentration in three-dimensional free-boundary Euler flow

paper.title: Cavity collapse and kinetic energy concentration in three-dimensional free-boundary Euler flow
paper.abstract:
Abstract. We construct smooth axisymmetric solutions of the three-dimensional
incompressible free-boundary Euler equations in bounded domains for
which a tubular cavity collapses onto a circle at a finite time T T .
The velocity has a single-valued potential, and the construction applies
without surface tension and with any fixed positive surface tension.
Both boundary components remain embedded and disjoint before collapse,
while the outer boundary converges smoothly. The terminal outer
meridional domain may be any smooth bounded simply connected domain
whose closure is separated from the rotation axis; the interior point
generating the collapse circle and the positive concentrated energy
may be prescribed independently. We prove a sharp collapse law with
radius asymptotic to an explicit multiple of ( T − t ) 1 / 2 | log ( T − t ) | − 1 / 4 (T-t)^{1/2}|\log(T-t)|^{-1/4} , determine curvature blow-up asymptotics,
and show that kinetic energy concentrates uniformly on the circle.
For a canonical reflection symmetric family, we identify a common
cylindrical spacetime limit and sharp velocity and pressure profiles.
At every fixed spatial point in the region enclosed by the limiting
outer boundary and away from the collapse circle, the velocity tends
to zero while the pressure tends to positive infinity. For this family,
we characterize the topology of the limiting material map and prove
its optimal 1 / 2 1/2 -Hölder regularity and sharp W 1 , p W^{1,p} threshold 1 ≤ p < 2 1\leq p<2 , with first derivatives in weak L 2 L^{2} but not in L 2 L^{2} .
These canonical solutions admit weak continuations that preserve mass
and momentum and whose total energy drops at collapse by exactly the
concentrated kinetic energy.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The geometry of a moving fluid domain can become singular even when the velocity remains irrotational. We study a collapse in which an entire free-boundary component contracts onto a curve: a tubular cavity in a bounded three-dimensional ideal fluid shrinks to a circle in finite time, while the outer free surface converges smoothly. The two boundary components remain embedded and disjoint at every time before collapse. The velocity has a single-valued potential throughout the evolution, so both vorticity and circulation vanish. Our main result constructs such flows with a prescribed terminal outer geometry and a prescribed positive amount of kinetic energy concentrating on the circle. The collapse rate is determined by the logarithmic capacity of a thin tube and depends, to leading order, only on the concentrated energy and the length of the circle. The construction works both without surface tension and for every fixed positive surface tension. The logarithmically corrected scaling already appears in the asymptotic potential-flow analysis of [ 22 ] . Here we realize it in the full three-dimensional Euler evolution of two free boundaries and determine its leading constant from the concentrated energy and the length of the collapse circle. Related hollow-vortex implosions [ 9 ] occur in planar exterior domains with nonzero circulation and a gas-pressure law. Our bounded, globally potential flows allow the terminal outer geometry and the concentrated energy to be prescribed independently within the class specified below. For a canonical reflection symmetric family, we further connect the concentration of energy to the degeneration of the material map and to the exact energy loss in a weak continuation on the filled domain. sections.heading: 1.1. Main results
sections.text: Theorem 1.1 gives the construction for prescribed terminal geometry, together with the collapse law, curvature asymptotics and energy concentration. The subsequent results concern the canonical reflection symmetric trajectories of Definition 1.4 : they determine the singular profiles, the terminal material map and the weak filling continuations.

sections.heading: 1.2. Relation to previous work
sections.text: The construction connects the potential-flow theory of cavity collapse with the analysis of singularities in the free-boundary Euler equations. We first discuss the closest collapse models, then place the result among other mechanisms of breakdown and the local theories used here.

sections.heading: 1.2.1. Cavity collapse and potential flows
sections.text: Classical radial models describe spherical cavity collapse. Rayleigh calculated the collapse of a spherical cavity in an infinite incompressible liquid under constant pressure at infinity [ 34 ] . Plesset extended the radial equation to account for time-dependent ambient pressure and a bubble boundary condition incorporating vapor pressure and surface tension [ 33 ] . For symmetric axisymmetric bubble pinch-off, the asymptotic potential-flow analysis of Gordillo–Sevilla–Rodríguez-Rodríguez–Martínez-Bazán [ 22 ] yields the logarithmically corrected relation T − t ≍ a 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / a ) T-t\asymp a^{2}\sqrt{\log(1/a)} , where a a is the dimensionless minimum neck radius and T T is the pinch-off time. Eggers–Fontelos–Leppinen–Snoeijer’s slender-body theory [ 18 ] evolves both the radial and axial scales and predicts a local radial exponent approaching 1 / 2 1/2 at order | log ( T − t ) | − 1 / 2 |\log(T-t)|^{-1/2} . Best’s boundary-integral computations describe toroidal bubbles formed after jet penetration [ 4 ] . Planar potential flows provide exact solutions and numerical models for singular boundary motion. Liu–Pego [ 26 ] analyze explicit ideal potential flows and investigate a corner formation scenario through scaling and time reversal of numerical flows expanding from smooth approximations to a wedge. Zhuravleva–Zubarev–Zubareva–Karabut [ 41 ] construct exact planar cavity flows with zero gravity and zero surface tension through a Hopf equation for the inverse complex velocity. The ballistic cavity examples analyzed in [ 26 , Section 6] occupy unbounded fluid domains and satisfy p < 0 p<0 in the fluid and ∂ n p = 0 \partial_{n}p=0 on the free boundary. Chen–Walsh–Wheeler [ 9 ] construct self-similarly imploding hollow vortices by desingularizing nondegenerate configurations of collapsing point vortices. Their flows are planar exterior flows with nonzero circulation around the cavities and a gas-pressure law on their boundaries.

sections.heading: 1.2.2. Free-boundary singularities
sections.text: Self-contact is a mechanism for free-boundary singularity formation. Castro–Córdoba–Fefferman–Gancedo–Gómez-Serrano constructed two-dimensional irrotational flows forming splash and splat singularities at zero surface tension [ 6 ] and at positive surface tension [ 5 ] . Coutand–Shkoller constructed three-dimensional splash and splat singularities at zero surface tension, allowing vorticity [ 13 ] . The authors [ 29 ] construct finite-time self-intersection singularities for the three-dimensional free-boundary ideal MHD equations with positive surface tension, with curvature controlled up to contact. The construction also yields capillary Euler self-intersection when the magnetic field vanishes. For two-dimensional irrotational water waves at zero surface tension, Córdoba–Enciso–Grubic [ 10 ] prove finite-time breakdown from initially cornered interfaces, through loss of weighted Sobolev regularity or self-intersection away from the corner. Agrawal [ 1 ] proves that a high-order energy becomes unbounded in finite time for zero-gravity water waves in a bounded planar domain with initially angle-crested interfaces. Coutand [ 11 ] proves finite-time breakdown for a planar two-phase flow in a fixed container, with gravity, surface tension and a heavier inner fluid, under symmetry and smallness assumptions on the initial geometry, velocities and outer fluid vorticity. In the solutions constructed here, an entire boundary component degenerates, with a quantitative curvature blow-up law, while the other component has a smooth limit. The initial boundaries are smooth, and both remain embedded and disjoint for every t < T t<T .

sections.heading: 1.2.3. Singularities on fixed domains
sections.text: For Euler flows on fixed domains, Elgindi constructed finite-time singularities on ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} for axisymmetric flows without swirl and with C 1 , α C^{1,\alpha} velocity, for a sufficiently small positive α \alpha [ 19 ] . Elgindi–Pasqualotto construct finite-energy axisymmetric flows with swirl whose initial velocity is C 1 , α C^{1,\alpha} for some α > 0 \alpha>0 and smooth away from a circle [ 20 , Theorem 1.3] . Their construction uses amplification driven by swirl near that circle. Chen–Hou [ 8 ] give an overview of their computer-assisted construction of nearly self-similar blow-up from smooth finite-energy data for axisymmetric Euler flows with swirl in an axially periodic cylinder with an impermeable wall. Chen constructs asymptotically self-similar blow-up on ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} for axisymmetric flows without swirl, with compactly supported C α C^{\alpha} initial vorticity and C 1 , α ∩ L 2 C^{1,\alpha}\cap L^{2} initial velocity for every 0 < α < 1 / 3 0<\alpha<1/3 [ 7 , Theorem 1.2] . These constructions develop singular vorticity in a fixed fluid domain. The recent manuscript of OpenAI [ 32 , Theorem 1.1] states finite-time breakdown on ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} from smooth, compactly supported initial velocity; Zheng [ 40 ] gives an expanded exposition of that construction. For smooth whole-space Euler flows, the Beale–Kato–Majda criterion [ 3 ] requires the time integral of the vorticity maximum norm to diverge at breakdown. In the present free-boundary problem, vorticity vanishes identically and the singularity is carried by the evolving geometry and the concentrating potential flow.

sections.heading: 1.2.4. Local theory and continuation
sections.text: For free-boundary Euler flows, local existence and a priori estimates have been developed in several settings. Iguchi and Ogawa–Tani established early local results at finite regularity for planar capillary–gravity flows [ 24 , 31 ] . Schweizer proved three-dimensional short-time existence for small periodic boundary graphs with initial vorticity vanishing on the free boundary [ 36 ] . Coutand–Shkoller established Sobolev existence theory at positive surface tension, with uniqueness for sufficiently regular data, and local well-posedness under the Taylor sign at zero surface tension [ 12 ] . Shatah–Zeng obtained geometric a priori estimates for the one-phase problem [ 38 ] and for capillary interfaces between two fluids [ 37 ] , and developed local well-posedness theory allowing vorticity and multiply connected fluid domains [ 39 ] . Disconzi–Kukavica [ 16 ] derive Lagrangian a priori estimates at the H 3 H^{3} bulk level with additional boundary trace regularity. Disconzi–Kukavica–Tuffaha [ 17 ] obtain H 5 / 2 + ε H^{5/2+\varepsilon} bulk estimates for 0 < ε < 1 / 2 0<\varepsilon<1/2 , including general bounded domains, with additional regularity of the initial boundary and normal velocity. Disconzi–Ebin [ 15 ] prove local well-posedness at positive surface tension. For irrotational water waves, the Dirichlet–Neumann formulation and paradifferential symmetrization reduce the free-surface equations to a quasilinear dispersive system [ 2 , 14 ] . Lannes [ 25 ] gives a systematic treatment of the Dirichlet–Neumann operator and the water-wave equations. Ming–Zhang establish local well-posedness for gravity–capillary waves over a smooth bottom and prove the zero tension limit over a flat bottom [ 30 ] . Their linearized estimates are uniform in surface tension under a positive Lévy coefficient. Continuation criteria connect finite-time breakdown to the loss of geometric or analytic control. At zero surface tension, Ginsberg’s criterion combines boundary geometry and the Taylor sign with vorticity, boundary velocity derivatives and a boundary pressure derivative norm [ 21 ] . Luo–Zhou obtain a criterion based on vorticity, coupled to boundary control norms and graph nondegeneracy for a horizontally periodic capillary surface above a fixed bottom [ 27 ] . For general bounded capillary domains, Hao and the authors give four breakdown alternatives involving boundary self-intersection, curvature and boundary regularity, normal velocity, and the time integral of the interior velocity gradient supremum [ 23 , Theorem 1.1 and Remark 1.2] .

sections.heading: 1.3. Mechanism and proof strategy
sections.text: The leading motion is governed by a logarithmic potential in the two directions normal to the collapse circle. Its gradient is proportional to the inverse distance from the circle, so its kinetic energy is distributed over a logarithmic range of radii. Energy conservation therefore fixes the amplitude of this potential and, through the kinematic condition, the collapse rate. The leading singular term is local; the outer geometry enters through the regular part of the Green function. Making this separation quantitative is what permits the prescription of an arbitrary outer meridional domain. Two difficulties remain beyond this leading description. The inner boundary shrinks while the outer boundary stays at a fixed scale, so the boundary equations must be estimated in different coordinates. Moreover, at positive surface tension the capillary coefficient in the rescaled equations tends to zero. The proof requires coercive estimates in the natural weighted norms, with a leading backward growth rate and fixed derivative losses independent of the Sobolev index. The constants in these estimates may depend on that index. We start from smooth terminal states with circular cavities of radii a N ↓ 0 a_{N}\downarrow 0 and solve backwards in Y = log ⁡ ( ℓ / a ) Y=\log(\ell/a) on [ Y 0 , Y N ] [Y_{0},Y_{N}] , where Y N = log ⁡ ( ℓ / a N ) Y_{N}=\log(\ell/a_{N}) . The central task is to choose Y 0 Y_{0} independently of N N and of the fixed regularity level at which compactness is taken. Step 1. Separate the flux and the geometric perturbations. The potential splits orthogonally in Dirichlet energy into a flux-carrying condenser field and a zero-flux remainder. For the normalized inner flux q = ( 2 ​ π ​ L ) − 1 ​ ∫ Γ − v ⋅ n ​ 𝑑 S q=(2\pi L)^{-1}\int_{\Gamma_{-}}v\cdot n\,dS , where L = 2 ​ π ​ R L=2\pi R , the energy identity determines q q , and the capacity expansion gives q 2 ​ Y → E c / ( π ​ L ∗ ) q^{2}Y\to E_{c}/(\pi L_{*}) . Differentiation yields the flux equation; energy conservation also recovers the constant Bernoulli equation between the boundaries. The mean and first harmonic of the inner graph determine the radius and centre. The first potential harmonic remains a separate dynamical unknown. With this choice, the reference forcing of the scaled higher modes starts at order a 3 a^{3} , up to polynomial factors in Y Y . The zero-flux constraint removes the logarithmic monopole; its finite-rank variations must still be retained in the nonlinear estimates. Step 2. Control the energy as the capillary coefficient vanishes. For fixed σ > 0 \sigma>0 , the effective coefficient B q = σ ​ a / q 2 B_{q}=\sigma a/q^{2} tends to zero. The principal inner energy is uniformly equivalent to ‖ 𝔥 ‖ H s + B q ​ ‖ 𝔥 ‖ H s + 1 + ‖ π ‖ H s + 1 / 2 , \|\mathfrak{h}\|_{H^{s}}+\sqrt{B_{q}}\,\|\mathfrak{h}\|_{H^{s+1}}+\|\mathfrak{\pi}\|_{H^{s+1/2}}, where ( 𝔥 , π ) (\mathfrak{h},\mathfrak{\pi}) are the normalized inner variables constructed in Section 4 . Thus the extra derivative of 𝔥 \mathfrak{h} carries a vanishing capillary weight. Two cancellations are essential. The inner Taylor coefficient, reconstructed from the Euler pressure, and the logarithmic flux derivative contain the same capacity correction, which cancels at leading logarithmic order in their coupling. In normal variables and surface half-densities, the principal Dirichlet–Neumann and curvature symbols are powers of the same arclength frequency. Commuting with powers of that frequency cancels the leading capillary commutator and gives a leading backward growth rate of 1 1 , independent of the Sobolev index. Zero-flux localization and a finite symbol expansion control the remainders. The fixed derivative losses and the coefficient regularity needed for these estimates are specified in Section 4 . The zero-flux localization in Proposition 4.2 applies to planar divergence-form equations with smooth uniformly positive scalar weights, homogeneous outer Dirichlet data, and a shrinking nearly circular hole uniformly separated from the outer boundary, under the stated uniform coefficient and geometric bounds. Step 3. Close the Taylor energies at zero surface tension. At σ = 0 \sigma=0 , both Taylor coefficients supply coercivity; the outer one is controlled by the limiting Green potential and Hopf’s lemma. Minimizing the outer Dirichlet–Neumann form over the constant inner trace enforces zero flux. We couple the inner energy at index s s to the outer energy at index s + 1 s+1 . The separated-boundary kernels allow high output derivatives on the outer boundary while using only a fixed lower norm of the inner input. The original outer Bernoulli equation gives the additional decay of the outer potential trace needed to close this coupling. Step 4. Obtain a common interval and pass to the collapsing limit. Coupling the inner and outer energies with suitable powers of the radius controls their mutual forcing. The leading backward growth rate is smaller than the decay exponent of the a 3 a^{3} inner forcing. This gives bounds independent of Y N Y_{N} with the same Y 0 Y_{0} at every fixed regularity. Compactness on nondegenerate intervals yields a smooth Euler trajectory, and the capacity law gives a finite collapse time. For prescribed outer geometry, retaining both centre coordinates and both first potential harmonics preserves these forcing orders and the distribution of derivatives between the boundaries. Step 5. Identify the singular profiles and the terminal material map. For the canonical trajectories, comparison with a truncated logarithmic potential determines the limiting line measure and its radial distribution. In particular, a tube whose radius is a fixed multiple of the cavity radius contains vanishing limiting energy: the concentration occurs over a logarithmic range of scales. The Green profile and the scaled collar estimates give the bulk pressure asymptotics and the cylindrical tangent, respectively. Subtracting boundary motion from the particle equation gives an equation with integrable coefficients for the difference of squared particle and boundary radii. The collar exit scale and volume preservation then yield the square-root normal form and the sharp derivative bounds for the terminal material map. Finally, integrable momentum and energy fluxes permit concatenation with a classical flow on the filled domain. Under the hypotheses of Proposition 5.13 (i), the incoming total-energy measure minus the outgoing one determines the local total-energy defect at the joining time. For the canonical continuations, the capillary-energy traces agree and the outgoing kinetic-energy trace vanishes. The defect is therefore the tensor product of the unit Dirac mass at the collapse time with the concentrated kinetic-energy measure on the collapse circle. Organization of the paper. Sections 2 – 4 develop the two-scale elliptic estimates, derive the exact boundary equations, and close the nonlinear energy estimates at positive surface tension. Section 5 constructs the canonical collapsing trajectory and proves its singular profiles, material map properties and filling continuation. Section 6 supplies the Taylor energies needed at zero surface tension and verifies the common inputs to these limiting arguments. Finally, Section 7 proves Theorem 1.1 for a prescribed outer section and core point by retaining both centre coordinates and both first potential harmonics.

sections.heading: 2. Two-scale Dirichlet–Neumann analysis
sections.text: For a single-valued axisymmetric velocity potential, the Laplace equation reduces to a planar divergence-form equation with a smooth weight. Using scaled coordinates near the inner boundary and physical coordinates near the outer boundary, we obtain uniform estimates for the layer potentials, the Dirichlet–Neumann operators and their first two shape variations. We then impose the zero-flux constraint by a Schur complement and derive the capacity and flux expansions used in the boundary dynamics. We write 𝒫 s ​ ( Y ) \mathcal{P}_{s}(Y) for a quantity bounded in absolute value by C s ​ ( 1 + Y ) M s C_{s}(1+Y)^{M_{s}} , where C s , M s ≥ 0 C_{s},M_{s}\geq 0 are constants. This quantity may change from one occurrence to the next and is chosen nonnegative in upper bounds. We suppress the argument Y Y when it is clear and omit the subscript at fixed lower regularity indices.

sections.text: We write the Euler equations in boundary variables and recover the flux from energy conservation. In centred polar coordinates, we estimate the first potential harmonic and determine the Taylor coefficients by reconstructing the pressure. We then derive the linearized system and prove the energy and terminal estimates used in the nonlinear construction.

Localization of the zero-flux Dirichlet–Neumann operator and paralinearization in normal variables reduce the problem to coupled inner and outer energy estimates.

sections.heading: 5. Terminal approximation and singular limit
sections.text: Using the uniform estimates of Theorem 4.13 , we let the terminal cavities shrink to obtain a canonical collapsing trajectory with positive surface tension. We derive its curvature, velocity, energy and pressure asymptotics, describe the terminal material map and the cylindrical limit, and construct a weak filling continuation with its exact energy defect. The limiting arguments also apply to the zero-surface-tension trajectories constructed in Section 6 .

sections.text: We prove Theorem 1.1 by adapting the canonical construction to the prescribed outer geometry. We first introduce the centred coordinates and the corresponding geometric estimates. The proof then applies the preceding elliptic and energy estimates while retaining both centre coordinates and both first potential harmonics.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.23605v1 [math.AP] 16 Oct 2026 Cavity collapse and kinetic energy concentration in three-dimensional free-boundary Euler flow Tao Luo and Siqi Yang Address: Tao Luo Department of Mathematics, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China Email address: taoluo@cityu.edu.hk Address: Siqi Yang School of Mathematics, Statistics and Mechanics, Beijing University of Technology, Beijing 100124, China Email address: siqiyang@bjut.edu.cn Abstract. We construct smooth axisymmetric solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible free-boundary Euler equations in bounded domains for which a tubular cavity collapses onto a circle at a finite time T T . The velocity has a single-valued potential, and the construction applies without surface tension and with any fixed positive surface tension. Both boundary components remain embedded and disjoint before collapse, while the outer boundary converges smoothly. The terminal outer meridional domain may be any smooth bounded simply connected domain whose closure is separated from the rotation axis; the interior point generating the collapse circle and the positive concentrated energy may be prescribed independently. We prove a sharp collapse law with radius asymptotic to an explicit multiple of ( T − t ) 1 / 2 | log ( T − t ) | − 1 / 4 (T-t)^{1/2}|\log(T-t)|^{-1/4} , determine curvature blow-up asymptotics, and show that kinetic energy concentrates uniformly on the circle. For a canonical reflection symmetric family, we identify a common cylindrical spacetime limit and sharp velocity and pressure profiles. At every fixed spatial point in the region enclosed by the limiting outer boundary and away from the collapse circle, the velocity tends to zero while the pressure tends to positive infinity. For this family, we characterize the topology of the limiting material map and prove its optimal 1 / 2 1/2 -Hölder regularity and sharp W 1 , p W^{1,p} threshold 1 ≤ p < 2 1\leq p<2 , with first derivatives in weak L 2 L^{2} but not in L 2 L^{2} . These canonical solutions admit weak continuations that preserve mass and momentum and whose total energy drops at collapse by exactly the concentrated kinetic energy. Key words and phrases: Free-boundary Euler equations, cavity collapse, blow-up, energy concentration, weak continuation 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification Primary 35Q31; Secondary 35B44, 35R35, 76B03 1. Introduction The geometry of a moving fluid domain can become singular even when the velocity remains irrotational. We study a collapse in which an entire free-boundary component contracts onto a curve: a tubular cavity in a bounded three-dimensional ideal fluid shrinks to a circle in finite time, while the outer free surface converges smoothly. The two boundary components remain embedded and disjoint at every time before collapse. The velocity has a single-valued potential throughout the evolution, so both vorticity and circulation vanish. Our main result constructs such flows with a prescribed terminal outer geometry and a prescribed positive amount of kinetic energy concentrating on the circle. The collapse rate is determined by the logarithmic capacity of a thin tube and depends, to leading order, only on the concentrated energy and the length of the circle. The construction works both without surface tension and for every fixed positive surface tension. The logarithmically corrected scaling already appears in the asymptotic potential-flow analysis of [ 22 ] . Here we realize it in the full three-dimensional Euler evolution of two free boundaries and determine its leading constant from the concentrated energy and the length of the collapse circle. Relation to previous work The construction connects the potential-flow theory of cavity collapse with the analysis of singularities in the free-boundary Euler equations. We first discuss the closest collapse models, then place the result among other mechanisms of breakdown and the local theories used here. 1.2.1. Cavity collapse and potential flows Classical radial models describe spherical cavity collapse. Rayleigh calculated the collapse of a spherical cavity in an infinite incompressible liquid under constant pressure at infinity [ 34 ] . Plesset extended the radial equation to account for time-dependent ambient pressure and a bubble boundary condition incorporating vapor pressure and surface tension [ 33 ] . For symmetric axisymmetric bubble pinch-off, the asymptotic potential-flow analysis of Gordillo–Sevilla–Rodríguez-Rodríguez–Martínez-Bazán [ 22 ] yields the logarithmically corrected relation T − t ≍ a 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / a ) T-t\asymp a^{2}\sqrt{\log(1/a)} , where a a is the dimensionless minimum neck radius and T T is the pinch-off time. Eggers–Fontelos–Leppinen–Snoeijer’s slender-body theory [ 18 ] evolves both the radial and axial scales and predicts a local radial exponent approaching 1 / 2 1/2 at order | log ( T − t ) | − 1 / 2 |\log(T-t)|^{-1/2} . Best’s boundary-integral computations describe toroidal bubbles formed after jet penetration [ 4 ] . Planar potential flows provide exact solutions and numerical models for singular boundary motion. Liu–Pego [ 26 ] analyze explicit ideal potential flows and investigate a corner formation scenario through scaling and time reversal of numerical flows expanding from smooth approximations to a wedge. Zhuravleva–Zubarev–Zubareva–Karabut [ 41 ] construct exact planar cavity flows with zero gravity and zero surface tension through a Hopf equation for the inverse complex velocity. The ballistic cavity examples analyzed in [ 26 , Section 6] occupy unbounded fluid domains and satisfy p < 0 p<0 in the fluid and ∂ n p = 0 \partial_{n}p=0 on the free boundary. Chen–Walsh–Wheeler [ 9 ] construct self-similarly imploding hollow vortices by desingularizing nondegenerate configurations of collapsing point vortices. Their flows are planar exterior flows with nonzero circulation around the cavities and a gas-pressure law on their boundaries. 1.2.2. Free-boundary singularities Self-contact is a mechanism for free-boundary singularity formation. Castro–Córdoba–Fefferman–Gancedo–Gómez-Serrano constructed two-dimensional irrotational flows forming splash and splat singularities at zero surface tension [ 6 ] and at positive surface tension [ 5 ] . Coutand–Shkoller constructed three-dimensional splash and splat singularities at zero surface tension, allowing vorticity [ 13 ] . The authors [ 29 ] construct finite-time self-intersection singularities for the three-dimensional free-boundary ideal MHD equations with positive surface tension, with curvature controlled up to contact. The construction also yields capillary Euler self-intersection when the magnetic field vanishes.
